betterCitation: Aemilia Lanyer, Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum, Eves Apologie, lines 5 and 6 of the stanza Then let vs haue our Libertie againe (1611)
reason: Attacked letter by letter against the 1611 first edition and it holds. The Early English Books scan was downloaded whole and read at the stanza, which prints: Then let vs haue our Libertie againe, / And challendge to your selues no Sou'raigntie; / You came not in the world without our paine, / Make that a barre against your crueltie; / Your fault beeing greater, why should you disdaine / Our beeing your equals, free from tyranny? / If one weake woman simply did offend, / This sinne of yours, hath no excuse, nor end. The doubled e of beeing in BOTH lines is the edition's own, against the modernised being that most transcriptions give, so the shipped spelling is right where a modernised text would have been wrong; disdaine, equals and tyranny? are as printed (the scan's stray stop after equals is optical noise for the comma). The locator is right: these are lines 5 and 6 of that stanza, under the running head and the marginal note Eues Apologie. The speaker trap was the real risk and it fails too. The section is not Pilate's wife speaking: the stanzas before it have the narrator address Pilate, O noble Gouernour ... But heare the words of thy most worthy wife, and the stanza just after our lines says Witnesse thy wife (O Pilate) speakes for all, in the third person, so the voice is the poem's own speaker pleading for women, and no parenthetical speaker is owed. Scope and publishability: 1611, imaginative literature, no scripture quoted, nothing needing a warning, and the claim of equality is the month's theme. Tag Poetry. shipped.js: nothing shipped, no near opening, aemilia lanyer 0 of 3, not banned. Source line 121 characters, leads with the name, no dash. Only improvement offered: name the two lines inside the stanza, which still fits at 128 characters.
